grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: yo llevo; tú llevas; usted lleva. Yo espero; tú esperas; Elena espera.
grammar.note_en:
A verb is a word expressing an action or state. This chapter changes who performs an action. Yo means “I”, the person speaking; tú means “you” when speaking informally to one person; usted is a respectful or formal “you” for one person. Ana and Luis use tú together. Ana first uses usted with the unfamiliar neighbour; after names and cooperation establish the relationship, they use tú. Usted is not a plural word.

The dictionary form of a verb is its infinitive, the form used to name the verb without saying who does it. Regular verbs whose infinitive ends in -ar share a present-tense pattern. Remove -ar and add -o for yo, -as for tú, or -a for a name or usted. Llevar means “carry” or “take”; its stem is llev-. Yo llevo means “I carry”, tú llevas “you carry”, and Elena lleva “Elena carries”. Usted lleva uses the same form as Elena lleva even though it addresses the listener: “you carry”. Do not add the English ending -s to Spanish’s I or you forms; choose the Spanish ending for that person.

Esperar means “wait” in this scene. Yo espero en el patio means “I wait in the courtyard”; Tú esperas aquí means “You wait here”; Ana espera means “Ana waits”. The same present pattern appears in llamar, “call”; dejar, “leave or set down”; ayudar, “help”; and hablar, “speak”. Yo llamo means “I call”, Yo dejo el libro aquí means “I leave the book here”, Yo ayudo means “I help”, and Elena habla means “Elena speaks”. Llamar here means calling out a person’s name, not saying what your own name is; the latter uses a construction taught later.

Spanish often leaves out a subject pronoun when the verb ending and the situation identify the speaker. This chapter shows yo and tú more often to make the contrast visible, but they are not obligatory before every verb in ordinary speech. Llamo already indicates “I call”; espero indicates “I wait”. With lleva or espera, context identifies the named person or usted. Tú llevas los libros; yo llevo las sillas means “You carry the books; I carry the chairs”. The contrasting pronouns help divide the task.

Questions retain the same verb endings. ¿Tú ayudas? means “Will you help?” or “Are you helping?”, as the situation requires; it is still a Spanish present form. ¿Usted lleva la llave de la sala? means “Are you carrying the reading room key?” Sí means “yes”, with a written accent; gracias means “thank you”. Both are complete conversational responses. The opening ¿ makes the question visible before you reach its end.

Hoy means “today”; mañana means “tomorrow” here. Mañana can also mean “morning” in other constructions, but that is not its use in these sentences. La tarde is “the afternoon”; en la tarde is a normal expression in the Mexican setting. Hoy, en la tarde means “today in the afternoon”; mañana, en la tarde means “tomorrow afternoon”. A present form can describe an agreed plan when the time is explicit: Yo llevo la mesa hoy means “I am taking the table today”. This chapter does not introduce a new future-tense ending. The table is still in the red house when they agree to help; the agreement does not mean the table has already been moved.

Casa means “house”; calle is the street outside; a vecina is a female neighbour. Persona means “person” and is a feminine noun regardless of the person’s gender. Una persona entra means “A person enters”. Elena holds the room key and coordinates the books, chairs and table; that does not mean she owns the courtyard. The older red key and blue key keep their distinct purposes.

The second table also gives Yo ayudo hoy, “I am helping today”. The first table reads “I carry / you carry (informal) / you carry (formal)” and “I wait / you wait (informal) / Elena waits”.
